reminder: A manifold is orientable when its local orientations fit together into one global orientation.
definition: A smooth [manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ of dimension $n$ is orientable if it has an [atlas](c:atlas) in which every change of chart has positive [Jacobian determinant](c:jacobian-determinant). Equivalently, $M$ carries a nowhere vanishing $n$-form, that is, a [volume form](c:volume-form).
examples: The [sphere](c:sphere) $S^n$ is orientable.
The [torus](c:torus) is orientable.
Non-example: the [Möbius strip](c:mobius-strip) is not orientable, because an oriented frame that travels once around its core circle comes back reversed.
Non-example: the [real projective plane](c:real-projective-plane) is not orientable.

steps: Start with a smooth manifold and an atlas of charts.
Ask that every change of chart has positive Jacobian determinant.
A smooth manifold with such an atlas is orientable, and the positivity condition is the only addition.
links.why: Orientability is a yes-or-no condition on a smooth manifold, not new structure.

reminder: The osculating circle at a point of a curve is the circle that best approximates the curve there.
definition: Let $\gamma$ be a smooth [curve](c:curve) with [curvature](c:curvature) $\kappa\neq0$ at a point $p$. The osculating circle at $p$ is the [circle](c:circle) that has the same [tangent line](c:tangent-line) as $\gamma$ at $p$, lies in the plane that best fits $\gamma$ near $p$, and has radius $1/\kappa$. Its center lies on the side of the tangent line toward which $\gamma$ bends.
examples: For a circle of radius $r$, the osculating circle at every point is the circle itself.
For the parabola $y=x^2$ at the origin, $\kappa=2$, so the osculating circle has radius $1/2$ and center $(0,1/2)$.
Non-example: at the point $0$ of $y=x^3$ the curvature is $0$, so no osculating circle exists there; the tangent line plays its role.

reminder: The p-adic completion of an abelian group $A$ is the limit of the quotients $A/p^nA$.
definition: The $p$-adic completion of an abelian group $A$ is $A^\wedge_p=\varprojlim_n A/p^nA$, the [adic completion](c:adic-completion) of $A$ along the ideal $(p)$. For $A=\mathbb Z$ it gives the [p-adic integers](c:p-adic-integer). For a nilpotent space or a spectrum, the $p$-completion is the analogous object that sees only mod-$p$ homology.
examples: $\mathbb Z^\wedge_p=\mathbb Z_p$, the ring of [p-adic integers](c:p-adic-integer).
For a finite abelian group $A$, the $p$-adic completion is the $p$-primary part of $A$.
The $p$-completion of the sphere $S^n$ with $n\ge2$ has homotopy groups $\pi_k(S^n)\otimes\mathbb Z_p$ for each $k$.
Non-example: for $A=\mathbb Q$ the completion is $0$, not $\mathbb Q_p$, because $p^n\mathbb Q=\mathbb Q$ for every $n$.

steps: Take the ring $\mathbb Z$ and its ideal $(p)$ for a prime $p$.
Form the adic completion of an abelian group $A$ along $(p)$, which is $\varprojlim_n A/p^nA$.
This adic completion is the $p$-adic completion of $A$.
links.why: A p-adic completion is an adic completion for one chosen prime, so the general theory applies.

reminder: Every sequence with bounded values and gradients that tend to zero has a convergent subsequence.
definition: Let $\Phi$ be a $C^1$ [functional](c:functional) on a [Banach space](c:banach-space) $X$. $\Phi$ satisfies the Palais-Smale condition if every [sequence](c:sequence) $(u_n)$ in $X$ with $\Phi(u_n)$ bounded and $\Phi'(u_n)\to0$ in the dual space has a convergent subsequence. The limit of such a subsequence is a [critical point](c:critical-point) of $\Phi$.
examples: A $C^1$ function on $\mathbb R^n$ with $\Phi(u)\to\infty$ as $|u|\to\infty$ satisfies it, because bounded values force bounded points.
The energy functional of $-\Delta u=|u|^{p-1}u$ on $H^1_0(\Omega)$, with $\Omega$ bounded and $p$ subcritical, satisfies it.
Non-example: $\Phi(x)=e^x$ on $\mathbb R$ fails it, because $x_n=-n$ has $\Phi(x_n)\to0$ and $\Phi'(x_n)\to0$ but no convergent subsequence.

reminder: Parallel transport carries a vector along a curve so that its covariant derivative along the curve stays zero.
definition: Let $E\to X$ be a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) with a [connection](c:connection-on-a-bundle) $\nabla$ and let $\gamma:[0,1]\to X$ be a smooth curve. For $v$ in the [fiber](c:fiber) $E_{\gamma(0)}$ there is a unique section $s$ along $\gamma$ with $s(0)=v$ whose [covariant derivative](c:covariant-derivative) along $\gamma$ vanishes, $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}s=0$. Parallel transport along $\gamma$ is the linear map $v\mapsto s(1)$ from $E_{\gamma(0)}$ to $E_{\gamma(1)}$.
examples: In the plane with the flat connection, transport along any path keeps the components of a vector fixed.
On the unit sphere, transport around a geodesic triangle turns a tangent vector by the angle excess of the triangle.
Non-example: a vector that turns at a steady rate against a straight line in the plane is not parallel along that line, because its [covariant derivative](c:covariant-derivative) is not zero.

reminder: A partial isometry preserves norms on the orthogonal complement of its kernel and sends the kernel to zero.
definition: A [bounded operator](c:bounded-operator) $V$ on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ is a partial isometry if $\|Vx\|=\|x\|$ for every $x$ in the orthogonal complement of $\ker V$. Equivalently, $V^*V$ is an [orthogonal projection](c:orthogonal-projection), where $V^*$ is the [adjoint](c:adjoint-operator) of $V$. Then $V$ maps its initial space $(\ker V)^\perp$ isometrically onto its final space, the range of $V$.
examples: Every [unitary operator](c:unitary-operator) is a partial isometry, with initial space and final space equal to $H$.
The unilateral shift on $\ell^2$ is a partial isometry; its adjoint, the backward shift, kills the first basis vector.
Non-example: $\operatorname{diag}(1,\tfrac12)$ on $\mathbb C^2$ has zero kernel but shrinks the second basis vector, so it is not a partial isometry.

steps: Take a unitary operator $U$ on a Hilbert space $H$.
Its kernel is zero, so $(\ker U)^\perp=H$, and $U$ preserves every norm.
So $U$ is a partial isometry whose initial space and final space are both $H$.
links.why: A partial isometry is a unitary operator that may kill one closed subspace and miss another.

steps: Take an orthogonal projection $P$ onto a closed subspace $M$.
It fixes $M$ and kills $M^\perp$, so $P^*P=P$ is a projection.
Hence $P$ is a partial isometry with initial space $M$ and final space $M$.
links.why: Orthogonal projections are the simplest partial isometries; the general case lets the map carry the initial space onto a different final space.

reminder: A path is a sequence of distinct vertices in which each consecutive pair is joined by an edge.
definition: In a [graph](c:graph), a path is a sequence $v_0,v_1,\dots,v_k$ of pairwise distinct [vertices](c:vertex) such that $v_{i-1}v_i$ is an [edge](c:edge) for each $i$. The number $k$ of edges is the length of the path, and the path joins $v_0$ to $v_k$.
examples: In a triangle with vertices $a,b,c$, the sequence $a,b,c$ is a path of length $2$.
In a [tree](c:tree), any two vertices are joined by exactly one path.
Non-example: the sequence $a,b,a$ along one edge $ab$ is not a path, because the vertex $a$ repeats.
Non-example: the sequence $a,b,c,a$ in a triangle is a [cycle](c:cycle), not a path.

reminder: A Pell equation asks for integer solutions of $x^2-dy^2=1$ for a fixed positive integer $d$ that is not a square.
definition: For a positive integer $d$ that is not a perfect square, the Pell equation is the [Diophantine equation](c:diophantine-equation) $x^2-dy^2=1$ in [integers](c:integer) $x$ and $y$. It has infinitely many solutions, and the nontrivial ones come from the convergents of the [continued fraction](c:continued-fraction) of $\sqrt d$.
examples: $x^2-3y^2=1$ has the smallest positive solution $(2,1)$.
Non-example: for the square $d=4$, the equation $x^2-4y^2=1$ factors as $(x-2y)(x+2y)=1$ and has only the solutions $(\pm1,0)$.

reminder: A perfect set is closed and every one of its points is an accumulation point of the set.
definition: A subset $C$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space) is perfect if it is a [closed set](c:closed-set) and every point of $C$ is an [accumulation point](c:accumulation-point) of $C$. Equivalently, $C$ is closed and has no [isolated point](c:isolated-point). The empty set counts as perfect.
examples: The closed interval $[0,1]$ is a perfect subset of $\mathbb R$.
The Cantor ternary set is perfect, although it contains no interval.
Non-example: $\{0\}\cup\{1/n:n\ge1\}$ is closed but not perfect, because each point $1/n$ is isolated.
Non-example: the open interval $(0,1)$ is not perfect, because it is not closed in $\mathbb R$.

steps: Take a closed set $C$ in a topological space.
Add the condition that every point of $C$ is an accumulation point of $C$.
A closed set that meets this condition is perfect.
links.why: A perfect set is a closed set with no isolated points, so every fact about closed sets still applies.

reminder: A graph is perfect when every induced subgraph has chromatic number equal to its clique number.
definition: A [graph](c:graph) $G$ is perfect if $\chi(H)=\omega(H)$ for every [induced subgraph](c:induced-subgraph) $H$ of $G$. Here $\chi$ is the [chromatic number](c:chromatic-number) and $\omega$ is the size of a largest [clique](c:clique). Always $\chi(H)\ge\omega(H)$, and perfection says this bound is tight for every induced subgraph.
examples: Every [complete graph](c:complete-graph) is perfect, because each induced subgraph is complete and has $\chi=\omega$.
Every [bipartite graph](c:bipartite-graph) is perfect.
Non-example: the $5$-cycle $C_5$ is not perfect, because $\chi(C_5)=3$ but $\omega(C_5)=2$.

steps: Take a bipartite graph $G$ and note that every induced subgraph of $G$ is again bipartite.
An induced subgraph with an edge has $\chi=\omega=2$.
An induced subgraph with no edge has $\chi=\omega=1$.
So every induced subgraph satisfies $\chi=\omega$, and $G$ is perfect.
links.why: Bipartite graphs are the first family of perfect graphs, and perfection keeps their colouring property.

reminder: A point of a function is periodic when applying the function a positive number of times returns the point.
definition: Let $f:X\to X$ be a [function](c:function). A point $x\in X$ is periodic if $f^n(x)=x$ for some integer $n\ge1$, where $f^n$ is the $n$-fold composition of $f$ with itself. The least such $n$ is the period of $x$, and a point of period $1$ is a [fixed point](c:fixed-point).
examples: For $f(x)=-x$ on $\mathbb R$, the point $1$ has period $2$.
For the rotation of the circle by the angle $2\pi p/q$ in lowest terms, every point has period $q$.
Non-example: for $f(x)=2x$ on $\mathbb R$, the point $1$ is not periodic, because its orbit $1,2,4,\dots$ never returns; only $0$ is periodic.

steps: Take a fixed point $x$ of $f$, so $f(x)=x$.
By induction, $f^n(x)=x$ for every $n\ge1$.
So $x$ is a periodic point of period $1$; periodic points also allow larger periods.
links.why: Fixed points are the period-1 case, so a result about periodic points covers fixed points too.

reminder: A place of a field is an equivalence class of nontrivial absolute values on that field.
definition: A place of a [field](c:field) $K$ is an equivalence class of nontrivial [absolute values](c:absolute-value) on $K$, where two absolute values are equivalent when they define the same topology on $K$. For a [number field](c:number-field), the places are the real and complex embeddings (the infinite places) and the nonzero [prime ideals](c:prime-ideal) of its ring of integers (the finite places).
examples: The field $\mathbb Q$ has one infinite place, from the usual absolute value, and one finite place for each prime $p$, from the $p$-adic absolute value.
The field $\mathbb Q(i)$ has one infinite place, a complex place, and its finite places match the prime ideals of $\mathbb Z[i]$.
Non-example: the trivial absolute value, with $|x|=1$ for every $x\neq0$, gives no place, because places use only nontrivial absolute values.

reminder: The Poincaré group is the group of isometries of Minkowski spacetime: translations combined with Lorentz transformations.
definition: The Poincaré group is the [isometry group](c:isometry-group) of [Minkowski space](c:minkowski-space) $\mathbb R^{d,1}$, that is, the group of affine maps that preserve the Minkowski metric. It is the [semidirect product](c:semidirect-product) $\mathbb R^{d+1}\rtimes O(d,1)$ of the translations with the [Lorentz group](c:lorentz-group) $O(d,1)$.
examples: A time translation $x\mapsto x+(t_0,0,0,0)$ belongs to the Poincaré group.
A boost along an axis and a rotation of space both belong to it.
Non-example: the rescaling $x\mapsto2x$ is not in the group, because it changes the Minkowski metric.

steps: Take the pseudo-Riemannian manifold $\mathbb R^{d,1}$ with the Minkowski metric.
Its isometry group is the group of maps that preserve this metric.
These maps are the translations composed with Lorentz transformations, which gives the Poincaré group.
links.why: The Poincaré group is the isometry group of one fixed spacetime, so general facts about isometry groups apply.

reminder: A map is point-surjective when every global element of its target is the image of a global element of its source.
definition: A morphism $f:X\to Y$ in a [category](c:category) with a [terminal object](c:terminal-object) $1$ is point-surjective if every [global element](c:global-element) $y:1\to Y$ equals $f\circ x$ for some global element $x:1\to X$.
examples: In the category of sets, a map is point-surjective exactly when it is surjective, because global elements are elements.
In the category of groups, the only global element of a group is its unit, so every homomorphism is point-surjective, even when it is not surjective.
Non-example: the inclusion $\{0\}\to\{0,1\}$ of sets is not point-surjective, because the element $1$ has no preimage.

steps: Work in the category of sets, where the terminal object is a one-point set.
A global element $1\to Y$ is the same as an element of $Y$.
So $f$ is point-surjective exactly when every element of $Y$ is a value of $f$, that is, when $f$ is surjective.
links.why: Point-surjectivity is the categorical form of surjectivity that Lawvere's fixed point theorem uses.

reminder: Polar coordinates describe a point other than the origin by its distance from the origin and its direction.
definition: Polar coordinates on $\mathbb R^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}$ describe a point $x$ by its distance $r=|x|>0$ from the origin and the point $u=x/|x|$ of the [unit sphere](c:unit-sphere) $S^n$, so that $x=ru$. The map $(r,u)\mapsto ru$ is a [coordinate system](c:coordinate-system) on [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) minus the origin. In the plane, $(x,y)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ where $\theta$ is the [angle](c:angle) from the positive $x$-axis.
examples: The point $(1,1)$ has polar coordinates $r=\sqrt2$ and $\theta=\pi/4$.
In the plane, the area element $dx\,dy$ becomes $r\,dr\,d\theta$.
Non-example: the origin has $r=0$ for every $\theta$, so polar coordinates are not a coordinate system at the origin.

steps: Take the open set $(0,\infty)\times(0,2\pi)$ of the plane.
Send the pair $(r,\theta)$ to the point $(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$.
This map is a smooth bijection onto the plane minus a ray, with smooth inverse, so it is a coordinate system.
links.why: Polar coordinates are a coordinate system adapted to rotation, which is why rotation-symmetric problems simplify.

reminder: The polynomial hierarchy stacks complexity classes by alternating quantifiers over polynomial-time checks, starting from P.
definition: Put $\Sigma_0^P=\mathrm P$ and $\Sigma_{k+1}^P=\mathrm{NP}^{\Sigma_k^P}$, that is, [NP](c:np-complexity-class) with an [oracle](c:oracle-machine) for a language in $\Sigma_k^P$, and let $\Pi_k^P$ hold the complements of the languages in $\Sigma_k^P$. The polynomial hierarchy is the union $\mathrm{PH}=\bigcup_k\Sigma_k^P$ of these [complexity classes](c:complexity-class). Equivalently, $\Sigma_k^P$ holds the languages that $k$ alternating quantifiers over strings of polynomial length define, starting with $\exists$, followed by a polynomial-time test.
examples: $\Sigma_1^P=\mathrm{NP}$ and $\Pi_1^P=\mathrm{coNP}$.
Deciding $\exists x\,\forall y\,\varphi(x,y)$ for a Boolean formula $\varphi$ is complete for $\Sigma_2^P$.
If $\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}$, then the whole hierarchy collapses to $\mathrm P$.
Non-example: the problem of true fully quantified Boolean formulas has no fixed number of alternations; it is PSPACE-complete and not known to lie in any level of the hierarchy.

steps: Take a language $L$ in NP, so $x\in L$ exactly when $\exists y\,R(x,y)$ for a polynomial-time test $R$.
This is one existential quantifier followed by a polynomial-time test, so $L\in\Sigma_1^P$.
Add more alternating quantifiers to get $\Sigma_2^P,\Sigma_3^P,\dots$, and take the union of all levels.
links.why: NP is the first level of the hierarchy, and the hierarchy adds further quantifier alternations on top of it.

reminder: A polynomial-time reduction turns an instance of one problem into an instance of another problem with the same answer.
definition: A polynomial-time reduction from a [language](c:language) $A$ to a language $B$ is a function $f$ that a polynomial-time [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) computes, such that $x\in A$ if and only if $f(x)\in B$ for every input $x$. We write $A\le_pB$ when such a reduction exists.
examples: SAT reduces to 3-SAT in polynomial time: split each long clause with new variables.
Every language $A$ in P reduces to every language $B$ that has both a member and a non-member: decide $x\in A$, then output a fixed member or a fixed non-member of $B$.
Composing two polynomial-time reductions gives a polynomial-time reduction, so $\le_p$ is transitive.

Non-example: a map that solves SAT by trying all assignments and then outputs a fixed yes-instance or no-instance has the right answers but runs in exponential time, so it is not a polynomial-time reduction.

reminder: The collapse map sends a framed tubular neighbourhood of a submanifold to a sphere and everything else to the point at infinity.
definition: Let $X$ be a compact [submanifold](c:submanifold) of a manifold $Y$ with [codimension](c:codimension) $n$, and let a [normal framing](c:normal-framing) identify a [tubular neighbourhood](c:tubular-neighbourhood) $U$ of $X$ with $X\times\mathbb R^n$. The Pontryagin-Thom collapse map is the map $Y\to S^n=\mathbb R^n\cup\{\infty\}$ that sends $(x,v)\in U$ to $v$ and every point outside $U$ to $\infty$. It is continuous, and $X$ is the preimage of the point $0$ of the [sphere](c:sphere).
examples: For $Y=S^n$ and $X$ a single framed point, the collapse map $S^n\to S^n$ has degree $\pm1$.
Pontryagin's theorem: collapse maps give a bijection between framed $k$-submanifolds of $S^{n+k}$, up to framed [cobordism](c:cobordism), and homotopy classes of maps $S^{n+k}\to S^n$.
Non-example: the core circle of a Möbius band has a nontrivial normal bundle, so it has no normal framing and no collapse map to $S^1$ of this form.

reminder: The $i$-th Pontryagin class of a real vector bundle is, up to sign, the $2i$-th Chern class of its complexification.
definition: For a real [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $E$ over a space $X$, the $i$-th Pontryagin class is $p_i(E)=(-1)^ic_{2i}(E\otimes\mathbb C)$ in $H^{4i}(X;\mathbb Z)$, where $c_{2i}$ is a [Chern class](c:chern-class) and $E\otimes\mathbb C$ is the [complexification](c:complexification) of $E$. These are the [characteristic classes](c:characteristic-class) of real bundles that come from the [classifying space](c:classifying-space) $BO(n)$.
examples: A trivial bundle has $p_i=0$ for every $i\ge1$.
The tangent bundle of $\mathbb{CP}^2$ has $p_1=3x^2$, where $x$ generates $H^2(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb Z)$.
Non-example: the odd Chern classes $c_{2i+1}(E\otimes\mathbb C)$ of a complexified bundle are not Pontryagin classes; they have order at most $2$.

steps: A characteristic class assigns to each real vector bundle $E\to X$ a cohomology class of $X$, naturally under pullback.
Define $p_i(E)=(-1)^ic_{2i}(E\otimes\mathbb C)$ in $H^{4i}(X;\mathbb Z)$.
Complexification and Chern classes commute with pullback, so $p_i$ is natural and is a characteristic class.
links.why: Pontryagin classes are one named family of characteristic classes, so the general theory of such classes applies.

reminder: A function on a group is positive-definite when every matrix of its values $\varphi(x_j^{-1}x_i)$ is positive semidefinite.
definition: A function $\varphi:G\to\mathbb C$ on a [group](c:group) $G$ is positive-definite if, for all $x_1,\dots,x_n\in G$, the matrix $(\varphi(x_j^{-1}x_i))_{i,j}$ is [positive semidefinite](c:positive-semidefinite-matrix). When $G$ is a [topological group](c:topological-group), one also asks that $\varphi$ is continuous.
examples: Every character $\chi:G\to S^1$ is positive-definite, because $\sum_{i,j}c_i\bar c_j\chi(x_j^{-1}x_i)=|\sum_ic_i\chi(x_i)|^2\ge0$.
The Gaussian $\varphi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}$ on $\mathbb R$ is positive-definite.
The [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function) of a probability measure on $\mathbb R^n$ is positive-definite.
Non-example: the indicator function of $[-1,1]$ on $\mathbb R$ is not positive-definite; for the points $0,1,2$ its matrix has determinant $-1$.

steps: Take a positive-definite function $\varphi$ on a group $G$.
Define the kernel $K(x,y)=\varphi(y^{-1}x)$ on $G\times G$.
The matrices $(K(x_i,x_j))$ are exactly the matrices of the definition, so they are positive semidefinite and $K$ is a positive-definite kernel.
links.why: A positive-definite function is a translation-invariant positive-definite kernel on a group, so kernel methods apply.

reminder: A positive operator on a complex Hilbert space satisfies $\langle Ax,x\rangle\ge0$ for every vector $x$.
definition: A [bounded operator](c:bounded-operator) $A$ on a complex [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ is positive if $\langle Ax,x\rangle\ge0$ for every $x\in H$. Such an operator is automatically [self-adjoint](c:self-adjoint-operator), and its [spectrum](c:spectrum-of-an-operator) lies in $[0,\infty)$. Equivalently, $A=B^*B$ for some bounded operator $B$.
examples: Every orthogonal projection $P$ is positive, because $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$.
For every bounded operator $B$, the operator $B^*B$ is positive, because $\langle B^*Bx,x\rangle=\|Bx\|^2$.
A diagonal matrix with nonnegative entries is a positive operator on $\mathbb C^n$.
Non-example: $-I$ is self-adjoint but not positive, because $\langle -x,x\rangle=-\|x\|^2<0$ for $x\neq0$.

steps: Take a positive operator $A$ on a complex Hilbert space.
Because $\langle Ax,x\rangle$ is real for all $x$, polarization gives $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,Ay\rangle$, so $A$ is self-adjoint.
The extra condition of the special case is $\langle Ax,x\rangle\ge0$, which puts the spectrum in $[0,\infty)$.
links.why: A positive operator is a self-adjoint operator with nonnegative spectrum, so spectral theory for self-adjoint operators applies.

steps: Take a positive semidefinite matrix $M$ of size $n\times n$ over $\mathbb C$.
View $M$ as a bounded operator on the Hilbert space $\mathbb C^n$.
The condition $x^*Mx\ge0$ is the same as $\langle Mx,x\rangle\ge0$, so $M$ is a positive operator.
links.why: Positive operators extend positive semidefinite matrices from $\mathbb C^n$ to any Hilbert space.

reminder: A prefix code is a set of codewords in which no codeword is the beginning of another codeword.
definition: A prefix code over an alphabet is a set $C$ of finite [words](c:word) such that no word of $C$ is a prefix of a different word of $C$. Every prefix code is a [uniquely decodable code](c:uniquely-decodable-code), and a decoder can read a message symbol by symbol with no look-ahead.
examples: $\{0,10,110,111\}$ is a prefix code over the alphabet $\{0,1\}$.
A code in which all words have the same length is a prefix code.
Huffman codes are prefix codes.
Non-example: $\{0,01\}$ is not a prefix code, because $0$ is a prefix of $01$; it is still uniquely decodable, but a decoder must look ahead.

steps: Take a message that is a concatenation of codewords from a prefix code $C$.
Read from the left; only one codeword matches the start, because no codeword extends another.
Remove that codeword and repeat, so the message splits in exactly one way and $C$ is uniquely decodable.
links.why: A prefix code is a uniquely decodable code that needs no look-ahead, so every prefix code is safe to use.

reminder: A proper ideal $Q$ is primary if $ab\in Q$ and $a\notin Q$ force some power of $b$ into $Q$.
definition: A proper [ideal](c:ideal) $Q$ of a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ is primary if $ab\in Q$ and $a\notin Q$ imply $b^n\in Q$ for some $n\ge1$. Equivalently, every zero-divisor of $R/Q$ is [nilpotent](c:nilpotent-element). The [radical](c:radical) $P=\sqrt Q$ of a primary ideal is a [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal), and $Q$ is then called $P$-primary.
examples: In $\mathbb Z$, the ideal $(p^n)$ is primary for a prime $p$ and $n\ge1$, with radical $(p)$.
In $k[x,y]$, the ideal $(x,y^2)$ is primary with radical $(x,y)$.
Non-example: in $k[x,y]$, the ideal $(x^2,xy)$ is not primary, although its radical $(x)$ is prime, because $x\cdot y\in(x^2,xy)$ and $x\notin(x^2,xy)$, but no power of $y$ lies in it.

steps: Take a prime ideal $P$ and elements with $ab\in P$ and $a\notin P$.
Primeness gives $b\in P$, so the power $b^1$ lies in $P$.
So $P$ is primary; the primary condition only asks that some power of $b$ lies in the ideal.
links.why: Primary ideals weaken prime ideals just enough to describe the pieces of a primary decomposition.

reminder: The prime factorization of an integer $n\ge2$ writes $n$ as a product of primes, unique up to order.
definition: A prime factorization of an [integer](c:integer) $n\ge2$ is an expression $n=p_1p_2\cdots p_k$ in which every $p_i$ is a [prime number](c:prime-number). Every $n\ge2$ has one, and it is unique up to the order of the factors; this is [unique factorization](c:unique-factorization) in $\mathbb Z$. Collecting equal factors gives $n=\prod_pp^{e_p}$.
examples: $60=2\cdot2\cdot3\cdot5=2^2\cdot3\cdot5$.
A prime $p$ is its own prime factorization, with one factor.
Non-example: $12=2\cdot6$ is not a prime factorization, because $6$ is not prime.
Non-example: in $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, $6=2\cdot3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ with all four factors irreducible, so uniqueness fails outside $\mathbb Z$.

steps: Take the ring $\mathbb Z$, which is an integral domain.
Its irreducible elements, up to sign, are the prime numbers.
Every nonzero non-unit factors into irreducibles, uniquely up to order and sign, so $\mathbb Z$ is a unique factorization domain.
links.why: Prime factorization in the integers is the model case of factorization in any unique factorization domain.

reminder: A probability distribution says how much probability each set of values of a random variable receives.
definition: The distribution of a [random variable](c:random-variable) $X:\Omega\to E$ is the [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\mu_X(B)=P(X\in B)$ on the value space $E$, which is the [pushforward measure](c:pushforward-measure) of $P$ under $X$. More generally, a probability distribution on a measurable space $E$ is any probability measure on $E$.
examples: A fair coin has the distribution on $\{0,1\}$ with $\mu(\{0\})=\mu(\{1\})=\tfrac12$.
The [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution) $N(0,1)$ has the [density](c:probability-density-function) $\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}$.
The [uniform distribution](c:uniform-distribution) on $[0,1]$ has density $1$ on that interval.
Non-example: Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$ is not a probability distribution, because its total mass is infinite.

steps: Take real numbers $m$ and $\sigma>0$.
Define the measure $B\mapsto\int_B\frac1{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-m)^2/2\sigma^2}\,dx$ on $\mathbb R$.
Its total mass is $1$, so it is a probability distribution, called the normal distribution.
links.why: Named distributions such as the normal distribution are probability distributions with a fixed density formula.

steps: Take a number $p$ with $0\le p\le1$.
Put mass $p$ on the value $1$ and mass $1-p$ on the value $0$.
The total mass is $1$, so this is a probability distribution on $\{0,1\}$, called the Bernoulli distribution.
links.why: The Bernoulli distribution is the smallest nontrivial probability distribution, a model of one yes-or-no trial.

reminder: A distribution has product form when it is a normalizing constant times a product of factors, one for each component.
definition: A [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) $\pi$ on the states $s=(s_1,\dots,s_J)$ of a system of $J$ components has product form if $\pi(s)=\frac1G\prod_jf_j(s_j)$ for every allowed state $s$. Each factor $f_j$ depends only on the state $s_j$ of component $j$, and $G$ is a normalizing constant. For a network that a [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) models, a product-form stationary distribution makes the components behave as if [independent](c:independence), apart from constraints on the allowed states.
examples: In an open Jackson network of $J$ queues with traffic intensities $\rho_j<1$, the stationary distribution is $\pi(n)=\prod_j(1-\rho_j)\rho_j^{n_j}$.
In a closed Gordon-Newell network with $N$ customers, the stationary distribution is $\pi(n)=\frac1{G(N)}\prod_j\rho_j^{n_j}$ on the states with $\sum_jn_j=N$.
Non-example: two queues in series with a finite buffer between them, so that the first queue can block, usually have no product-form stationary distribution.

reminder: The projective dimension of a module is the length of its shortest projective resolution.
definition: The projective dimension of a [module](c:module) $M$ over a [ring](c:ring) $R$ is the least $n$ for which there is an [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) $0\to P_n\to\cdots\to P_0\to M\to0$ of [projective modules](c:projective-module) $P_i$. It is $\infty$ when no finite sequence of this kind exists. Equivalently, it is the least $n$ with $\operatorname{Ext}^{n+1}_R(M,-)=0$.
examples: A projective module has projective dimension $0$.
Over $\mathbb Z$, the module $\mathbb Z/n$ with $n\ge2$ has projective dimension $1$, from the sequence $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/n\to0$.
Over $k[x,y]$, the module $k=k[x,y]/(x,y)$ has projective dimension $2$.

Non-example: over $\mathbb Z/4$, the module $\mathbb Z/2$ has infinite projective dimension, because its resolution $\cdots\xrightarrow2\mathbb Z/4\xrightarrow2\mathbb Z/4\to\mathbb Z/2$ never ends in a projective module.

reminder: A pseudofunctor between bicategories preserves composition and identities only up to coherent invertible 2-cells.
definition: A pseudofunctor $F:\mathcal B\to\mathcal C$ between [bicategories](c:bicategory) sends objects, 1-morphisms and 2-morphisms to the same kinds, and it preserves composition of 2-morphisms strictly. It preserves [composition](c:composition) and [identities](c:identity-morphism) of 1-morphisms up to given [2-isomorphisms](c:2-isomorphism) $F(g)F(f)\Rightarrow F(gf)$ and $1_{F(x)}\Rightarrow F(1_x)$, which satisfy coherence laws. It is a [strict 2-functor](c:strict-2-functor) when all these 2-isomorphisms are identities.
examples: Every strict 2-functor is a pseudofunctor with identity comparison cells.

Sending a space $X$ to its category of vector bundles and a map $f$ to pullback $f^*$ is a pseudofunctor from spaces, with maps reversed, to categories, because $(gf)^*\cong f^*g^*$ only up to canonical isomorphism.
Non-example: a [lax functor](c:lax-functor) whose comparison cells $F(g)F(f)\Rightarrow F(gf)$ are not invertible is not a pseudofunctor.

steps: Take a strict 2-functor $F$, which preserves composition and identities exactly.
Use identity 2-cells as the comparison cells $F(g)F(f)\Rightarrow F(gf)$ and $1_{F(x)}\Rightarrow F(1_x)$.
Identities are invertible and satisfy the coherence laws, so $F$ is a pseudofunctor.
links.why: Every strict 2-functor is a pseudofunctor, and pseudofunctors allow invertible comparison cells in place of equalities.

steps: A lax functor has comparison 2-cells $F(g)F(f)\Rightarrow F(gf)$ that need not be invertible.
Ask that every comparison 2-cell is invertible.
A lax functor with this condition is a pseudofunctor.
links.why: A pseudofunctor is a lax functor with invertible comparison cells, so lax-functor results apply to it.

reminder: A qubit is a quantum state of a system whose state space is a two-dimensional complex Hilbert space.
definition: A qubit is a [quantum state](c:quantum-state) of a system whose state space is the two-dimensional [complex vector space](c:complex-vector-space) $\mathbb C^2$ with its inner product, a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space). A pure state is a unit vector $\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle$ with $|\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1$, taken up to a global phase.
examples: The spin of an electron is a qubit, with spin up and spin down as the basis states $|0\rangle$ and $|1\rangle$.
The state $\frac1{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)$ is a qubit state in an equal superposition of $|0\rangle$ and $|1\rangle$.
Non-example: a three-level system, called a qutrit, has a three-dimensional state space, so it is not a qubit.

steps: A qudit is a quantum state in a $d$-dimensional complex Hilbert space.
Fix the dimension to be $d=2$ in this definition.
The state space is then $\mathbb C^2$, and the qudit is a qubit.
links.why: A qubit is the two-level case of a qudit, so results for qudits specialize to qubits.

reminder: In a quasi-separated space, the intersection of any two compact open subsets is compact.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is quasi-separated if, for all [compact](c:compact-space) [open](c:open-set) subsets $U$ and $V$ of $X$, the intersection $U\cap V$ is compact.
examples: Every Noetherian space is quasi-separated, because every subset of it is compact.
The spectrum of any commutative ring is quasi-separated.

Non-example: infinite-dimensional affine space with a doubled origin is not quasi-separated; its two copies of affine space are compact open sets, but their intersection, affine space minus the origin, is not compact.

steps: Take a Hausdorff space $X$ and compact open sets $U$ and $V$.
In a Hausdorff space, compact sets are closed, so $V$ is closed in $X$.
Then $U\cap V$ is a closed subset of the compact set $U$, hence compact, so $X$ is quasi-separated.
links.why: Every Hausdorff space is quasi-separated, so the weaker condition holds in the usual analytic settings.

reminder: A quasiconformal map is an orientation-preserving homeomorphism whose complex dilatation is bounded away from one.
definition: A [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) $f:U\to V$ between domains in $\mathbb C$ is quasiconformal if it preserves orientation, has locally square-integrable weak derivatives, and satisfies the [Beltrami equation](c:beltrami-equation) $\partial_{\bar z}f=\mu_f\,\partial_zf$ almost everywhere with a [bounded function](c:bounded-function) $\mu_f$ such that $\|\mu_f\|_\infty=k<1$. The map is then $K$-quasiconformal with $K=\frac{1+k}{1-k}$, and the $1$-quasiconformal maps are the [conformal maps](c:conformal-map).
examples: Every conformal map is $1$-quasiconformal, because $\partial_{\bar z}f=0$.
The stretch $f(x+iy)=Kx+iy$ is $K$-quasiconformal: it has $\partial_zf=\frac{K+1}2$ and $\partial_{\bar z}f=\frac{K-1}2$, so $\mu_f=\frac{K-1}{K+1}$.
Non-example: the homeomorphism $f(x+iy)=x+iy^3$ of $\mathbb C$ is not quasiconformal, because $|\mu_f|\to1$ as $y\to0$.

steps: Take a conformal map $f$, which is a holomorphic homeomorphism between domains in $\mathbb C$.
Then $\partial_{\bar z}f=0$, so $\mu_f=0$ and $\|\mu_f\|_\infty=0<1$.
So $f$ is $1$-quasiconformal; general quasiconformal maps allow any $\mu_f$ with $\|\mu_f\|_\infty<1$.
links.why: Quasiconformal maps relax conformality to bounded angle distortion, and they keep the Beltrami equation as the control.

reminder: An R-matrix is an invertible operator on $V\otimes V$ that solves the Yang-Baxter equation.
definition: An R-matrix on a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ is an invertible element $R$ of $\operatorname{End}(V\otimes V)$, built with the [tensor product](c:tensor-product), that solves the [quantum Yang-Baxter equation](c:quantum-yang-baxter-equation) $R_{12}R_{13}R_{23}=R_{23}R_{13}R_{12}$ in $\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes3})$. Here $R_{ij}$ acts on the $i$-th and $j$-th factors. Then $PR$, with $P$ the flip of the two factors, satisfies the braid relation, so $R$ gives a representation of the [braid group](c:braid-group) on $V^{\otimes n}$.
examples: The flip $P(u\otimes v)=v\otimes u$ is an R-matrix, and it gives the action of the symmetric group.
The standard R-matrix of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ on $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$ gives braid group representations that lead to the Jones polynomial.
Non-example: the zero map on $V\otimes V$ solves the equation but is not invertible, so it is not an R-matrix.

reminder: A rational cone is a cone in $\mathbb R^n$ generated by finitely many vectors with rational coordinates.
definition: A rational cone is a set $C=\{\lambda_1v_1+\cdots+\lambda_mv_m:\lambda_i\ge0\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ where $v_1,\dots,v_m$ are vectors with [rational](c:rational-number) coordinates. Equivalently, it is a [convex cone](c:convex-cone) that is the intersection of finitely many half-spaces $\{x:a\cdot x\ge0\}$ with rational vectors $a$.
examples: The first quadrant of $\mathbb R^2$ is generated by $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$, so it is a rational cone.
The cone generated by $(1,0)$ and $(1,2)$ is a rational cone.
Non-example: the cone generated by $(1,0)$ and $(1,\sqrt2)$ is not rational, because its edge through $(1,\sqrt2)$ has no nonzero rational point.

steps: A convex cone is a set closed under sums and under multiplication by nonnegative reals.
Take a convex cone generated by finitely many vectors.
Ask that the generators have rational coordinates; the cone is then a rational cone.
links.why: Rationality ties a convex cone to the integer lattice, which is what lattice-point counting needs.

reminder: The real part of a complex number $z$ is $(z+\bar z)/2$, the first coordinate of $z$.
definition: For a [complex number](c:complex-number) $z=a+bi$ with $a$ and $b$ [real](c:real-number), the real part is $\operatorname{Re}z=a=\tfrac12(z+\bar z)$, where $\bar z$ is the [complex conjugate](c:complex-conjugation) of $z$. More generally, in a [star-algebra](c:star-algebra) of characteristic zero, the real part of $x$ is $\tfrac12(x+x^*)$.
examples: $\operatorname{Re}(3-4i)=3$, and $\operatorname{Re}(i)=0$.
The real part of a real number is the number itself.
For a square complex matrix $M$ with the conjugate transpose as star, the real part $\tfrac12(M+M^*)$ is the Hermitian part of $M$.
Non-example: the modulus is not the real part, because $|3-4i|=5$ while $\operatorname{Re}(3-4i)=3$.

reminder: A reduced word in an HNN extension has no subword that the defining relations can shorten.
definition: Let $G*_\varphi=\langle G,t\mid t^{-1}at=\varphi(a)\ (a\in A)\rangle$ be an [HNN extension](c:hnn-extension) of a [group](c:group) $G$, where $\varphi:A\to B$ is an isomorphism of [subgroups](c:subgroup) of $G$. A word $g_0t^{\epsilon_1}g_1\cdots t^{\epsilon_n}g_n$ with $g_i\in G$ and $\epsilon_i=\pm1$ is reduced if it has no pinch, that is, no subword $t^{-1}g_it$ with $g_i\in A$ and no subword $tg_it^{-1}$ with $g_i\in B$. Britton's lemma says that a reduced word with $n\ge1$ is not the identity of $G*_\varphi$.
examples: A word $g_0\in G$ with no letter $t$ is reduced, because it has no subword to shorten.
In $\langle a,t\mid t^{-1}at=a^2\rangle$, the word $tat^{-1}$ is reduced, because $a\notin\langle a^2\rangle$; so it is not the identity.
Non-example: in the same group, $t^{-1}at$ is not reduced, because it is a pinch and equals $a^2$.

reminder: A reflective subcategory is a full subcategory whose inclusion functor has a left adjoint.
definition: A [full subcategory](c:full-subcategory) $\mathcal D$ of a [category](c:category) $\mathcal C$ is reflective if the inclusion $\mathcal D\to\mathcal C$ has a left [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) $L$, called the reflector. So each object $X$ of $\mathcal C$ has a universal map $\eta_X:X\to LX$ into an object of $\mathcal D$, and every map from $X$ to an object of $\mathcal D$ factors uniquely through $\eta_X$.
examples: Abelian groups form a reflective subcategory of groups, and abelianization is the reflector.
Compact Hausdorff spaces form a reflective subcategory of topological spaces, and the Stone-Čech compactification is the reflector.
Sheaves form a reflective subcategory of presheaves, and sheafification is the reflector.
Non-example: fields form a full subcategory of commutative rings, but the inclusion has no left adjoint, because $\mathbb Z$ has no universal ring map to a field.

reminder: A Banach space is reflexive when the natural map from the space into its double dual is onto.
definition: A [Banach space](c:banach-space) $X$ is reflexive if the canonical map $J:X\to X^{**}$, given by $J(x)(f)=f(x)$, is surjective. Here $X^{**}$ is the [bidual](c:bidual), the [dual space](c:dual-space) of $X^*$. Then $J$ is an isometric isomorphism, so $X$ and $X^{**}$ are identified.
examples: Every finite-dimensional normed space is reflexive.
The space $L^p$ with $1<p<\infty$ is reflexive, because its dual is $L^q$ with $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$.
Non-example: $c_0$ is not reflexive, because $c_0^*=\ell^1$ and $c_0^{**}=\ell^\infty$ is strictly larger than $c_0$.

steps: Take a Hilbert space $H$, which is a Banach space for its norm.
The Riesz representation theorem identifies $H^*$ with $H$, so $H^{**}$ is also identified with $H$.
Hence every element of $H^{**}$ is evaluation at a vector of $H$, so $J$ is onto and $H$ is reflexive.
links.why: Reflexivity is the property of Hilbert spaces that survives in Banach spaces such as $L^p$.

reminder: The relative interior of a convex set is its interior taken inside the affine hull of the set.
definition: For a [convex set](c:convex-set) $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, the relative interior $\operatorname{ri}C$ is the [interior](c:interior) of $C$ in its affine hull, the smallest [affine subspace](c:affine-subspace) that contains $C$. A point $x$ lies in $\operatorname{ri}C$ when some [ball](c:ball) $B(x,\varepsilon)$ has $B(x,\varepsilon)\cap\operatorname{aff}C\subseteq C$.
examples: For the segment $[a,b]$ in $\mathbb R^2$, the relative interior is the open segment $(a,b)$, while the interior in $\mathbb R^2$ is empty.
For a single point $\{p\}$, the relative interior is $\{p\}$.
Non-example: an endpoint $a$ of the segment $[a,b]$ is not in the relative interior, because every ball around $a$ meets the line outside the segment.

steps: Take a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ whose affine hull is all of $\mathbb R^n$.
Then the topology of the affine hull is the usual topology of $\mathbb R^n$.
So the interior of $C$ in its affine hull is the usual interior of $C$.
links.why: For sets that span the whole space nothing changes, and the relative interior repairs the empty interior of flat sets.

reminder: An interaction is renormalizable when finitely many parameters fix the counterterms that cancel its divergences at all orders.
definition: In perturbative quantum field theory, an interaction, a [local observable](c:local-observable) built from the fields, is renormalizable if the freedom in its [renormalization](c:renormalization) is fixed by finitely many real parameters. By power counting, this holds when every interaction term has mass dimension at most the spacetime dimension $d$.
examples: The $\phi^4$ interaction of a scalar field is renormalizable in spacetime dimension $4$.
The coupling $\bar\psi\gamma^\mu A_\mu\psi$ of quantum electrodynamics is renormalizable in dimension $4$.
Non-example: the $\phi^6$ interaction is not renormalizable in dimension $4$, because its term has mass dimension $6>4$ and each order needs new counterterms.

reminder: The resolvent cubic of a quartic has as roots the three sums $r_1r_2+r_3r_4$ over the ways to split its roots into pairs.
definition: Let the monic quartic $x^4+ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ have [roots](c:root-of-a-polynomial) $r_1,r_2,r_3,r_4$. Its resolvent cubic is the [cubic polynomial](c:cubic) with the roots $r_1r_2+r_3r_4$, $r_1r_3+r_2r_4$ and $r_1r_4+r_2r_3$. Its coefficients are [polynomial](c:polynomial) expressions in $a,b,c,d$: it equals $y^3-by^2+(ac-4d)y-(a^2d-4bd+c^2)$.
examples: For $x^4-5x^2+4$, with roots $1,-1,2,-2$, the resolvent cubic is $y^3+5y^2-16y-80=(y+5)(y-4)(y+4)$.
For $x^4-1$, the resolvent cubic is $y^3+4y$, with roots $0$ and $\pm2i$.
Non-example: the discriminant is a single number, not a cubic polynomial, although the quartic and its resolvent cubic have the same discriminant.

reminder: An object $A$ is a retract of $B$ when maps $A\to B\to A$ compose to the identity of $A$.
definition: An object $A$ of a [category](c:category) is a retract of an object $B$ if there are morphisms $i:A\to B$ and $r:B\to A$ such that $r\circ i$ is the [identity](c:identity-morphism) of $A$. Then $r$ is a retraction and $i$ is a [section](c:section) of $r$. For a subspace $A$ of a topological space $X$, this means a continuous map $r:X\to A$ that fixes every point of $A$.
examples: Every object is a retract of itself, with $i=r=\mathrm{id}$.
The circle is a retract of the punctured plane, by the map $x\mapsto x/|x|$.
Every nonempty set is a retract of each of its supersets, by sending the new points to one fixed point.
Non-example: the circle $S^1$ is not a retract of the closed disc $D^2$, by Brouwer's no-retraction theorem.

steps: Take a deformation retraction of $X$ onto a subspace $A$, which is a homotopy $H$ from $\mathrm{id}_X$ to a map into $A$ that fixes $A$.
Set $r(x)=H(x,1)$; it maps $X$ into $A$ and fixes each point of $A$.
So $r\circ i=\mathrm{id}_A$ and $A$ is a retract; a deformation retract adds the homotopy $\mathrm{id}_X\simeq i\circ r$.
links.why: Retracts forget the homotopy, so retract results apply to every deformation retract.

reminder: A rewriting system is a set of objects with rules that replace one object by another in one step.
definition: A rewriting system consists of a [set](c:set) $A$ of objects and a reduction relation $\to$ on $A$, where $a\to b$ means that $a$ can be rewritten to $b$ in one step. Usually the steps come from rules: in a string rewriting system, $A$ is the set of [words](c:word) over an alphabet, and a rule $\ell\to r$ replaces any occurrence of $\ell$ in a word by $r$.
examples: The rule $ab\to\varepsilon$ on words over $\{a,b\}$ gives the steps $aabb\to ab\to\varepsilon$.
Simplification rules on arithmetic expressions, such as $2+3\to5$, form a rewriting system.
Non-example: the equation $ab=ba$ is not yet a rewriting system, because a step needs a direction; choose the rule $ba\to ab$.

reminder: A ring has an addition that forms an abelian group and an associative multiplication with identity that distributes over it.
definition: A ring is a set $R$ with addition and multiplication such that $(R,+)$ is an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) with zero $0$, $(R,\cdot)$ is a [monoid](c:monoid) with identity $1$, and multiplication satisfies the [distributive law](c:distributive-law) $a(b+c)=ab+ac$ and $(a+b)c=ac+bc$. A ring is [commutative](c:commutative-ring) when $ab=ba$ for all $a,b$.
examples: The integers $\mathbb Z$ with the usual operations form a ring.
The $n\times n$ real matrices form a ring, and it is not commutative for $n\ge2$.
The polynomials $k[x]$ over a field $k$ form a ring.
Non-example: the natural numbers $\mathbb N$ are not a ring, because $1$ has no additive inverse in $\mathbb N$, so $(\mathbb N,+)$ is not a group.

steps: A semiring has addition and multiplication, where addition is only a commutative monoid.
Ask that every element has an additive inverse, so that addition becomes an abelian group.
A semiring with this condition is a ring.
links.why: A ring is a semiring with additive inverses, so semiring results hold for rings.

steps: Take a commutative ring, whose addition is an abelian group and whose multiplication is associative with identity.
The multiplication also distributes over addition, so these are the ring axioms.
So every commutative ring is a ring; a general ring drops the condition $ab=ba$.
links.why: A ring need not be commutative, and this link shows which results need the commutativity.

reminder: The ring of integers of a number field is the set of its elements that are roots of monic polynomials with integer coefficients.
definition: The ring of integers $\mathcal O_K$ of a [number field](c:number-field) $K$ is the set of [algebraic integers](c:algebraic-integer) that lie in $K$, that is, the elements of $K$ that are roots of a monic [polynomial](c:polynomial) with integer coefficients. It is a [subring](c:subring) of $K$ and a [Dedekind domain](c:dedekind-domain) with fraction field $K$.
examples: For $K=\mathbb Q$, the ring of integers is $\mathbb Z$.
For $K=\mathbb Q(i)$, the ring of integers is $\mathbb Z[i]$, the Gaussian integers.
For $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)$, the ring of integers is $\mathbb Z[\frac{1+\sqrt5}2]$, which is larger than $\mathbb Z[\sqrt5]$.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z[\sqrt5]$ is not the ring of integers of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)$, because $\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$ is a root of $x^2-x-1$ but is not in $\mathbb Z[\sqrt5]$.

steps: Take $K=\mathbb Q$, a number field of degree $1$.
A rational number that is a root of a monic integer polynomial is an integer, by the rational root theorem.
So the ring of integers of $\mathbb Q$ is $\mathbb Z$, and the ring of integers of $K$ extends the integers to $K$.
links.why: The ring of integers plays the role of $\mathbb Z$ in a number field, though unique factorization may fail there.

reminder: A rotation matrix is a real orthogonal matrix with determinant $1$.
definition: A rotation matrix is a real [orthogonal matrix](c:orthogonal-matrix) $R$ whose [determinant](c:determinant) is $1$, so $R^TR=I$ and $R$ preserves lengths and orientation. The rotation matrices of size $n$ form the [special orthogonal group](c:special-orthogonal-group) $SO(n)$. In the plane, they are exactly the matrices $\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$.
examples: The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ is the rotation of the plane by $90^\circ$.
The identity matrix is a rotation matrix, with angle $0$.
Non-example: the reflection $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ is orthogonal, but its determinant is $-1$, so it is not a rotation matrix.

steps: Take an orthogonal matrix $Q$, so that $Q^TQ=I$ and $\det Q$ is $1$ or $-1$.
Add the condition $\det Q=1$, which rules out reflections.
An orthogonal matrix with this condition is a rotation matrix.
links.why: Rotations are the orientation-preserving half of the orthogonal matrices.

reminder: Scalar curvature is one function on a Riemannian manifold: the trace of its Ricci curvature.
definition: On a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) $(M,g)$ of dimension $n$, the scalar curvature is the [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $R=\operatorname{tr}_g\operatorname{Ric}$, the trace of the [Ricci curvature](c:ricci-curvature) with respect to the metric. At a point it equals $\sum_{i\neq j}K(e_i,e_j)$ for an orthonormal basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$, where $K$ is the [sectional curvature](c:sectional-curvature). So $R=n(n-1)K$ when the sectional curvature is a constant $K$.
examples: The unit sphere $S^n$ has $R=n(n-1)$.
Flat $\mathbb R^n$ has $R=0$, and hyperbolic space of curvature $-1$ has $R=-n(n-1)$.
Non-example: the product of the unit sphere $S^2$ and the hyperbolic plane has $R=2-2=0$ but is not flat, so scalar curvature does not determine the full curvature.

steps: Take a surface with a Riemannian metric, so that $n=2$.
At each point the only sectional curvature is the Gaussian curvature $K$.
The sum over ordered pairs gives $R=2K$, so scalar curvature extends Gaussian curvature to higher dimensions.
links.why: On a surface the scalar curvature is twice the Gaussian curvature, so surface results lift to all dimensions.

reminder: The Schur complement of a block in a block matrix is what remains after that block is eliminated.
definition: For a [block matrix](c:partitioned-matrix) $M=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}$ in which $A$ is square and [invertible](c:inverse-matrix), the Schur complement of $A$ in $M$ is $M/A=D-CA^{-1}B$. It satisfies $\det M=\det A\cdot\det(M/A)$ for the [determinant](c:determinant).
examples: For $M=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ with $A=(2)$, the Schur complement is $3-\frac12=\frac52$, and $\det M=5=2\cdot\frac52$.
In Gaussian elimination, clearing the first block column of $M$ leaves $D-CA^{-1}B$ in the lower right block.
A symmetric $M$ with $A$ [positive-definite](c:positive-definite-matrix) is positive-definite exactly when $M/A$ is positive-definite.
Non-example: if $A=(0)$ is not invertible, the expression $D-CA^{-1}B$ has no meaning, so the Schur complement of $A$ is not defined.

reminder: The Schwartz space holds the smooth functions on $\mathbb R^n$ whose derivatives all decay faster than any polynomial grows.
definition: The Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ is the set of [smooth functions](c:smooth-function) $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C$ on [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) with $\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|<\infty$ for all multi-indices $\alpha$ and $\beta$. It is a [Fréchet space](c:frechet-space) for the [seminorms](c:seminorm) $p_{\alpha,\beta}(f)=\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$, and the [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) maps it onto itself.
examples: The Gaussian $e^{-|x|^2}$ is a Schwartz function, and so is every polynomial times it.
Every smooth function with compact support is a Schwartz function.
Non-example: $f(x)=\frac1{1+x^2}$ on $\mathbb R$ is smooth but not Schwartz, because $x^3f(x)$ is unbounded.

steps: Take a Schwartz function $f$; it is smooth by definition.
Add the decay condition $\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|<\infty$ for all multi-indices $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
A smooth function that meets this condition is a Schwartz function.
links.why: A Schwartz function is a smooth function with rapid decay of all derivatives, so smooth calculus applies to it.

reminder: A function is lower semicontinuous when its value at a point is at most the limit inferior of its nearby values.
definition: A function $f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ on a [topological space](c:topological-space) is lower semicontinuous if $\{x:f(x)>a\}$ is open for every [real](c:real-number) $a$, and upper semicontinuous if $\{x:f(x)<a\}$ is open for every $a$. Lower semicontinuity at $x$ means $f(x)\le\liminf_{y\to x}f(y)$, using the [limit inferior](c:limit-inferior). A function is [continuous](c:continuous-function) exactly when it is both.
examples: The indicator function of an open set is lower semicontinuous, and that of a closed set is upper semicontinuous.
A supremum of continuous functions is lower semicontinuous.
Non-example: $f=1$ on $(-\infty,0]$ and $f=0$ on $(0,\infty)$ is not lower semicontinuous at $0$, because $f(0)=1$ exceeds $\liminf_{y\to0}f(y)=0$.

steps: Take a continuous function $f:X\to\mathbb R$.
For every real $a$, the set $\{f>a\}$ is the preimage of the open set $(a,\infty)$, so it is open.
So $f$ is lower semicontinuous, and likewise upper semicontinuous: continuity means both.
links.why: Semicontinuity splits continuity into two one-sided halves, which is enough for existence of minimizers.

reminder: A semiring has a commutative monoid addition and a monoid multiplication, where multiplication distributes over addition and $0$ annihilates.
definition: A semiring is a set $S$ with addition and multiplication such that $(S,+)$ is a [commutative monoid](c:add-comm-monoid) with identity $0$, $(S,\cdot)$ is a [monoid](c:monoid) with identity $1$, multiplication satisfies the [distributive law](c:distributive-law), and $0\cdot a=a\cdot0=0$. Some authors drop the identity $1$ or the annihilation law; this definition keeps both, and it is the structure that nLab calls a [rig](c:rig).
examples: The natural numbers $\mathbb N$ with the usual addition and multiplication form a semiring.
The Boolean semiring $\{0,1\}$ uses $\lor$ as addition and $\land$ as multiplication.
The tropical semiring $(\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\},\min,+)$ has zero $\infty$ and one $0$.
Non-example: $\mathbb N$ with $\max$ as addition and $+$ as multiplication satisfies distributivity, but the additive identity $0$ does not annihilate, since $0+a=a$.

steps: Take a ring $R$; its addition is an abelian group, so in particular a commutative monoid.
Its multiplication is associative with identity and distributes over addition.
In a ring $0\cdot a=0$ follows from distributivity, so all semiring laws hold and every ring is a semiring.
links.why: Semirings drop additive inverses, so they include the natural numbers and tropical algebra that rings exclude.
